title: The Enclosure Call
primary_metric: total cost per unit at the client's target first-year production volume (materials + amortized mold tooling + shipping)

options.A: Project Horn — the cone-frustum enclosure the audio engineer wants, with a costlier tapered mold and less efficient shipping stacking
options.B: Project Orb — the spherical enclosure the creative director wants, with a cheaper mold but real, well-known sphere-packing shipping waste

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4

deliverables.text: A dimensioned, labeled diagram of each enclosure option — Project Horn's cone frustum and Project Orb's sphere — with the 3-D shape of each correctly named and every dimension used in the calculations marked directly on the diagram.
A materials-cost table showing each option's total exterior surface area and the resulting material cost per unit.
A packing-and-shipping table showing each option's packing efficiency inside a standard shipping container, units per container, and shipping cost per unit.

A total-cost-per-unit comparison table combining materials (D2), amortized mold tooling, and shipping (D3) for Project Horn vs. Project Orb at the client's target production volume, with a stated recommendation.

balance.argument_a: Project Horn's tapered mold costs more up front, but the frustum shape stacks and nests far more efficiently for shipping than the sphere does. If Project Horn's shipping-cost-per-unit advantage over the client's target production run outweighs its higher amortized-tooling-cost-per-unit and its higher per-unit material cost (a larger tapered shell can mean more surface area than a sphere of comparable internal volume, depending on the exact dimensions in Appendix A), Project Horn wins on total cost per unit.
balance.argument_b: Project Orb's mold is simpler and cheaper to cut, and the sphere may have less exterior surface area than the frustum for a comparable internal volume, lowering its material cost. But a sphere can never exceed roughly 74% packing density in a container (the Kepler-conjecture ceiling), well below what a tapered or flat-sided shape can achieve — if that shipping penalty, multiplied across the client's full target production volume, outweighs Project Orb's tooling and material savings, Project Orb loses on total cost per unit despite its cheaper mold.
balance.margin_basis: Once Appendix A's dimensions and Appendix B/C's cost and packing figures are sourced: compute total cost per unit for each option as (surface area × material cost per sq in) + (mold tooling cost ÷ target production volume) + (freight cost per container ÷ (container volume × packing efficiency ÷ unit volume)), then compare Project Horn's and Project Orb's total cost per unit and express the gap as a percentage of the lower figure.
